prohibited_recommendations: Do not give scheduled or long-acting benzodiazepines; treat alcohol withdrawal symptom-triggered with the lowest effective dose of lorazepam or oxazepam and close monitoring of consciousness (EASL ALD 2018).
Do not prescribe opioids or other sedating drugs: they precipitate and prolong HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not transfuse to a hemoglobin above 8 g/dL: liberal transfusion raises portal pressure and the risk of rebleeding (Baveno VII).
required_recommendations: Variceal bleeding: vasoactive drug now (terlipressin, octreotide or somatostatin), ceftriaxone 1 g daily for up to 7 days, restrictive transfusion to hemoglobin 7-8 g/dL, upper endoscopy within 12 hours after resuscitation (Baveno VII); the penicillin allergy (rash) is not a contraindication: cross-reactivity with ceftriaxone is low; give with monitoring.
Protect the airway: intubate before endoscopy, given grade III HE with agitation and active upper GI bleeding (Baveno VII).
Blood, urine and ascitic cultures are drawn before the first antibiotic dose, which is not delayed for them.

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022), by nasogastric tube or retention enema while he cannot swallow safely; avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.
Add rifaximin 550 mg twice daily to lactulose for this recurrent overt episode (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).
Give parenteral thiamine before or with the dextrose that corrects the hypoglycemia (glucose 61 mg/dL), without delaying the glucose (daily heavy drinking, poor intake).
Replace potassium to 4.0 mEq/L or more, because hypokalemia increases renal ammoniagenesis, and replace magnesium (1.2 mg/dL) and phosphate (2.1 mg/dL) intravenously.

Hold propranolol, spironolactone, furosemide, metformin and lisinopril during the bleed (hypotension, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL); do not restart lisinopril, since ACE inhibitors are contraindicated with ascites (EASL 2018).
Monitor for alcohol withdrawal (daily heavy drinking, blood alcohol 142 mg/dL on arrival) and treat it symptom-triggered with the lowest effective dose of lorazepam or oxazepam (EASL ALD 2018).
After the acute course, start primary SBP prophylaxis (norfloxacin 400 mg daily or ciprofloxacin): ascitic protein 1.2 g/dL with Child-Pugh C and bilirubin above 3 mg/dL (EASL 2018).

Assess with hepatology for superimposed alcohol-related hepatitis (daily heavy drinking, bilirubin 8.7 mg/dL, AST 312 U/L); corticosteroids are considered only once bleeding and infection are controlled (EASL ALD 2018).
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with recurrent overt HE and variceal bleeding, MELD-Na 32 (EASL 2018), together with treatment for alcohol use disorder (EASL ALD 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 32), precipitated by upper GI hemorrhage, hypokalemia, recent alcohol use and lactulose non-adherence

differential.key_features: Excluded: ascitic PMN 180 cells/mm3, Gram stain negative, culture no growth; the leucocytosis is explained by the bleed and stress.
Blood alcohol 142 mg/dL on arrival makes current withdrawal unlikely; asterixis, fetor and triphasic waves indicate HE. Withdrawal may follow as the alcohol clears.

differential.diagnosis: Acute ethanol intoxication as the cause
differential.key_features: Contributes, but 142 mg/dL in a daily drinker does not explain asterixis, rigidity, Babinski signs and triphasic waves.
INR 2.8 and platelets 78; no trauma reported, no focal deficit, and CT shows no hemorrhage.
Myoclonic jerks raised the question; EEG shows triphasic waves on delta slowing without epileptiform discharges, and the jerks have no EEG correlate.
Daily drinking and poor intake; extraocular movements intact, no nystagmus. Not excluded; thiamine is given empirically.

key_clinical_evidence: Child-Pugh C (15: bilirubin 8.7 3, albumin 2.1 3, INR 2.8 3, moderate ascites 3, HE grade 3 3); MELD-Na 32 (creatinine 1.4, bilirubin 8.7, INR 2.8, sodium 128)
HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading, evidence of liver dysfunction and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleeding, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia, hyponatremia), constipation, sedatives, dehydration, kidney injury and non-adherence to lactulose (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).
When multiple precipitants coexist, all must be addressed simultaneously; fixing one in isolation will not resolve HE.
In variceal bleeding with altered consciousness, the airway is protected before endoscopy, and antibiotic prophylaxis is given to every patient with cirrhosis and GI bleeding (Baveno VII).

patient.history_present_illness: A 58-year-old man with known alcoholic cirrhosis was brought to the emergency department by his neighbor after being found confused and combative at home. According to the neighbor, the patient had been complaining of dark, tarry stools for approximately 24 hours prior to presentation. He was found sitting in a chair, unable to recognize his neighbor and shouting incoherently. Over the past few days, the patient had reportedly stopped eating, was not taking his lactulose as prescribed, and had continued drinking alcohol. His neighbor noted that his abdomen appeared more distended than usual. He had no known history of seizures or head trauma. On arrival to the ED, the patient was oriented only to his name, was agitated and pulling at IV lines, and could not provide a coherent history. He smelled strongly of alcohol. His skin was visibly jaundiced. He was tachycardic and hypotensive on arrival. Melena was found on rectal examination. No focal neurological deficits were identified on initial assessment, and there was no evidence of meningismus. The patient's daughter, reached by phone, confirmed he had a history of hepatic encephalopathy once before, two years ago following a GI bleed, which resolved with lactulose and rifaximin. She reported he had been increasingly confused over the past 48 hours and had refused to go to the hospital until his neighbor forced the issue today.

neurological_exam.additional: Jaundice visible in sclera and skin. Spider angiomata on chest. Gynecomastia. Palmar erythema. Caput medusae. Moderate ascites on abdominal exam. Fetor hepaticus present.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 4mm, equal, sluggishly reactive. Extraocular movements intact. No nystagmus. Facial symmetry preserved. Gag reflex intact but diminished.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to stand safely; ataxic on attempted transfer.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 12 (E3V4M5). Confused and combative, oriented to name only. Asterixis (flapping tremor) present bilaterally on sustained arm extension. Slurred speech. Unable to complete serial 7s or spell WORLD backwards.
neurological_exam.motor: Increased tone bilaterally. Moves all extremities spontaneously. Intermittent myoclonic jerks of the upper extremities.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 2+ throughout. Bilateral Babinski signs present.
neurological_exam.sensory: Unable to cooperate with full sensory exam. Withdraws to pain symmetrically.
